story.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump's Mail Voting Restrictions, Sparks His Criticism
story.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court has rejected efforts by Donald Trump to impose new restrictions on mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections. This ruling allows states to continue using existing mail voting procedures. Following the decision, Trump criticized the court and specifically called out Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas for their dissenting opinions.

event_overview.title: About Mail Voting
event_overview.subject: Mail Voting
event_overview.summary: Mail voting, also called absentee voting in many jurisdictions, is the use of ballots sent to voters and returned through the mail. In the United States, states and local election officials generally set voter eligibility, ballot-counting rules, and deadlines, while the U.S. Postal Service handles the mailing and delivery of election materials and has issued federal-mailing standards for ballots used in federal elections.

facts.label: What counts as Election Mail
facts.value: USPS defines Election Mail as material sent to or from authorized election officials that enables participation in voting; Ballot Mail is the subset containing a live ballot.

facts.label: Who administers voting by mail
facts.value: The Constitution provides that state legislatures prescribe the times, places, and manner of congressional elections, subject to Congress's authority to make or alter those regulations. USPS says state and local officials—not the Postal Service—determine mail-voting eligibility and whether returned ballots may be counted.

facts.label: Federal protections for overseas and mil
facts.value: Federal law requires states to permit absent uniformed-services voters and overseas citizens to vote by absentee ballot in federal general, special, primary, and runoff elections; where no delivery preference or applicable state-law method exists, the ballot is transmitted by mail.

facts.label: 2026 USPS ballot-mail rule
facts.value: USPS published a final rule, effective August 21, 2026, that sets mailpiece-preparation and data-reporting standards for mail-in or absentee ballots in federal elections. The rule states that it regulates use of the mail rather than voter eligibility or ballot counting, and refers to the November 3, 2026 federal general election.

facts.label: Practical delivery context
facts.value: USPS advises voters to follow their jurisdiction's rules and deadlines and, as a general precaution, to mail completed domestic ballots at least one week before the deadline by which the election office must receive them; state receipt and postmark rules differ.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected timeline focuses on the September 2026 controversy, litigation, and federal USPS requirements surrounding ballot mail ahead of the midterms; it does not cover every state's mail-voting law, all forms of absentee voting, or the broader history of election administration.

explore_lenses.label: What was blocked—and what was not?
explore_lenses.title: New USPS conditions are paused
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling did not alter states’ underlying mail-voting laws. It left in place a nationwide preliminary injunction against a new USPS rule that would have imposed mandatory federal-ballot-mail design, barcode, and data-submission conditions.

claims.text: The Supreme Court denied the government’s request to stay the preliminary injunction, finding the government unlikely to succeed in challenging it at this interim stage.

The blocked USPS rule would have required envelopes for federal-election ballots to use the Official Election Mail logo, be compatible with high-speed processing, and carry a specialized voter-specific barcode; election officials also would have had to submit designs and voter-mailing data through a USPS portal.
Under the rule, USPS would have returned noncompliant outbound ballot mailings to the authorized election mailer for correction rather than accepting them.

USPS’s existing election-mail guidance already recommends several of these features, including the election-mail logo and serialized Intelligent Mail barcodes; the disputed rule would have made specified requirements mandatory for federal ballots.

explore_lenses.label: Why did the justices split?
explore_lenses.title: Timing and legal authority drove the dispute
explore_lenses.summary: The Court’s brief order focused on the government’s weak showing for emergency relief. Justice Kavanaugh said USPS may ultimately possess relevant authority, but concluded that implementing the rule for the November 3, 2026 election would be unlawful because officials lacked reasonable time to comply.

claims.text: Justice Kavanaugh concurred in denying a stay because applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act given the limited time for state and local implementation.

Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, dissented. They argued that the government met the requirements for a stay, challenged the plaintiffs’ standing, and maintained that USPS has broad statutory authority to regulate mail and adopt the rule.

The administration characterized the requirements as modest standards intended to improve ballot-mail visibility, support enforcement against potential fraud, and preserve public confidence; it said USPS would not determine voter eligibility.
The district court concluded that election officials said full compliance was likely impossible on the timetable and that refusing noncompliant mailings could substantially disenfranchise voters.

explore_lenses.label: What happens before the midterms?
explore_lenses.title: The injunction remains while litigation continues
explore_lenses.summary: For now, the mandatory rule cannot be enforced for the November 3, 2026 midterms. The underlying appeal and merits litigation remain pending, while USPS may continue voluntary portal and design-related work permitted by the lower court.

claims.text: The Supreme Court’s September 14, 2026 order leaves the preliminary injunction in force, so the rule’s mandatory requirements remain on hold pending further litigation.
The government sought a stay pending proceedings in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit and possible further Supreme Court review.

USPS said it may continue building the Federal Ballot Mail Portal and communicating about envelope-design standards on a voluntary basis; it said verification before mail acceptance was not being performed under the court order.

Forecast: The government argued that, if the injunction were later lifted, states that had not taken preparatory steps could face difficulty using mail ballots under the rule; this is the government’s litigation position, not a court finding.

story_report.summary: The Supreme Court denied the government’s bid to enforce a new U.S. Postal Service rule for federal-election ballot mail, leaving a preliminary injunction in place. The September 14 order means the mandatory envelope, barcode and portal requirements cannot be imposed while litigation continues, allowing election officials to use current mail-voting processes rather than comply with the blocked federal rule. Trump criticized the court after the decision and noted the dissenting justices.

sections.heading: Blocked Postal Service Ballot Rule
sections.body: The USPS rule would have required federal-election ballot envelopes to display the Official Election Mail logo, work with high-speed processing equipment and carry a voter-specific barcode. Election officials also would have been required to submit envelope designs and voter-mailing data through a USPS portal. USPS already recommends some of those practices, but the contested rule would have made specified standards mandatory and required noncompliant outbound ballot mailings to be returned for correction.

sections.heading: Justices Divided on Election Timing
sections.body: Justice Kavanaugh concurred in denying a stay, concluding that implementing the rule for the 2026 elections would likely be arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local officials had limited time to comply. Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, dissented, arguing that the government met the stay standard, that the plaintiffs lacked standing and that USPS has broad authority to regulate mail. The administration described the standards as modest safeguards for ballot-mail visibility, fraud enforcement and public confidence, while saying USPS would not decide voter eligibility.

sections.heading: Federal Ballot Mail Litigation Continues
sections.body: The government sought a stay while the case proceeds in the First Circuit and potentially returns to the Supreme Court. USPS has said it may continue developing its Federal Ballot Mail Portal and provide voluntary guidance on envelope standards, but it is not verifying mailings before acceptance under the court order. A district court found that election officials viewed full compliance on the timetable as likely impossible and that rejected mailings could substantially disenfranchise voters.

unresolved.text: The emergency order does not finally decide whether USPS may adopt a similar rule for a future election cycle, and the available record does not establish whether the First Circuit will rule on the merits before the election.
The ruling addresses enforcement of the USPS rule, rather than resolving the validity of each state’s separate procedures for requesting, casting or counting mail ballots.
